content: A Water Safety Plan (WSP) is designed to identify and manage risks to drinking water quality throughout the entire water supply chain, from the source to the consumer's tap. However, traditional WSPs often do not address risks that may arise after water reaches the household, such as contamination during collection, storage, or treatment within the home. This manual provides detailed guidance on conducting household surveys as part of a WSP, particularly for organized piped water supply systems in resource-limited settings. Specific examples and tools, such as a survey planning checklist, are included in the appendices. Preparation Before Starting the Survey To successfully implement a household survey for a WSP, it is essential to have a thorough understanding of the water delivery system, the survey area, and the population being served. Before beginning, gather relevant information to guide the development of the questionnaire and support the final report. Some of this data, such as water quality information, may already be available from the WSP system description. Additional data can be obtained from health departments, surveillance teams, laboratory staff, or community health workers. Population Data Obtain detailed maps of the community or district, with defined boundaries and known population sizes. Use the most recent census data for population estimates, preferably broken down by clusters. Identify alternative water sources (e.g., private wells, rivers, springs, bottled water, rainwater) and their specific uses (e.g., drinking versus other purposes). Health Department Data Determine the number of hospitals and clinics (both public and private) serving the area. Assess whether a surveillance system is in place. Gather regional or national estimates for diarrhea or gastrointestinal (GI) disease incidence. Investigate any known, suspected, or perceived health problems associated with water quality, including anecdotal evidence. Allocate time for data cleaning, analysis, and report writing, which may take several weeks. Present and review the data with the WSP team early in the process, ideally alongside other system assessment activities. Budget Planning Interviewers may be compensated on a daily basis or per completed questionnaire. If payment is per questionnaire, a small daily base rate should also be provided, along with compensation for visits where interviews were not completed due to the occupants being unavailable or refusing to participate. This approach encourages adherence to visitation protocols. Field managers should receive a slightly higher daily rate than interviewers. Drivers should be paid a daily rate that includes the cost of fuel and phone calls. Transportation costs should also account for sample transport to laboratories if needed. Provide interviewers and field coordinators with phone cards or credit to facilitate communication about protocol issues or security concerns. To prevent overuse, consider using a daily call log or providing credit incrementally. If microbiological testing is required, include costs for laboratory processing or field test kits. Additional supplies, such as collection bottles, labels, and coolers, will also be necessary. Data Entry Hire one or two detail-oriented individuals to enter completed questionnaires into a database. Data entry should ideally occur daily to address ambiguities promptly. If resources allow, double data entry is recommended to minimize errors. If double entry is not feasible, more extensive data cleaning will be required before analysis. Sampling Methodology Calculate an appropriate sample size using statistical tools, such as the sample size and power calculator in Epi Info. This calculation should account for the population size, expected frequency of the outcome variable, and the acceptable margin of error. For example, if diarrhea prevalence is estimated at 15%, a sample size should be large enough to detect a difference of ±5% with 95% confidence. Add approximately 10% to the sample size to account for non-respondents. If a higher non-response rate is anticipated, increase this percentage accordingly. Use random or stratified systematic sampling methods to select households. If a household is unoccupied or declines to participate, record this information and visit the next closest household. Recruitment and Training of Survey Teams Recruit a survey team with a clear composition of roles, including interviewers, field managers, and drivers. Household Survey Content The survey should collect information on: Household demographics (e.g., age, education, socioeconomic status, household size). Water sources for drinking and other uses. Consistency and quality of piped water service (e.g. Household water storage practices (e.g., tanks, buckets, pitchers). Water treatment methods (e.g., boiling, filtration, chlorination). Perceptions of water quality, customer satisfaction, and health risks. Costs of water service and payment systems. Sanitation and hygiene practices (e.g., toilet types, handwashing). Health issues among household members (e.g., diarrhea, skin infections, access to healthcare). Water quality parameters, such as chlorine residuals and microbiological contamination. Reporting and Presentation of Results Survey results should be reported systematically, following the structure of the survey instrument. Key sections should include: Demographics of respondents. Description of water sources and service, including alternative sources. Household storage and treatment practices. Sanitation and hygiene practices. Community concerns and health issues. Water quality results, with comparisons between tap water, stored water, and drinking water containers. Appendices The manual includes several appendices with practical tools, such as: A checklist for survey planning. A sample budget estimate. A template for informed consent. A method for calculating sample size. A sample household visitation log sheet. By following these detailed guidelines, the household survey can provide valuable insights into water safety risks and inform targeted interventions to improve water quality and public health outcomes.
